title: Memphis Dry Rub Ribs
subtitle: Pork spare ribs cooked without sauce, finished with the rub
excerpt: Memphis dry ribs are cooked without any sauce, relying entirely on the spice rub for flavour. The rub is applied before cooking, and again as a dusting at the end. What you get is a rib with a deeply spiced crust, the meat tender and smoky-tasting from slow oven heat.
sourceNotes: Memphis dry-style ribs are a recognised regional American barbecue tradition from Tennessee, defined by the absence of sauce and the double application of dry rub. Adapted here for the home oven.

recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap in foil and freeze. Reheat at 160°C covered for 20 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Apply the rub and refrigerate the rack uncovered for up to 24 hours before cooking. The dry salt will pull moisture out and back in, deepening the flavour.

content.text: Memphis dry ribs are the austere end of the American rib spectrum: no sauce, no glaze, just meat and spice. The rub goes on twice, before and after cooking, and the flavour comes from the spices setting into the surface over long, low heat. The result is a rack with a firm, fragrant crust and juicy meat beneath that needs nothing added at the table.

Heat the oven to 150°C (fan 130°C / gas mark 2). Combine all the rub ingredients and mix well. Remove the membrane from the bone side of the {{pork-ribs}}: loosen a corner with a blunt knife and peel it off with kitchen paper.
Pat the rack completely dry. Press the rub all over both sides and the edges, using about three quarters of the mixture. Reserve the rest for finishing.

Place the rack meat side up on a foil-lined baking tray. Cover tightly with foil. Cook at 150°C for two and a half to three hours, until the meat has pulled back from the bone ends and feels soft when pressed.
Remove the foil and increase the oven to 180°C (fan 160°C / gas mark 4). Cook uncovered for a further 30 minutes until the surface is set and dark in places.
Remove from the oven and dust the meat side generously with the reserved dry rub. This second application goes on hot: the residual heat and fat on the surface help it adhere and bloom the spices.
Rest for ten minutes. Cut between the bones and serve. On the table in Memphis, dry ribs are often served with a small bottle of hot sauce and sliced white bread: nothing more.

items.symptom: The surface rub falls off the hot rack
items.cause: Not enough residual fat or moisture on the surface to help it stick.
items.fix: Brush the surface lightly with a thin coat of rapeseed oil before adding the finishing rub. The rub should cling within seconds.

items.symptom: The ribs taste dry without any sauce
items.cause: Overcooked or cooked at too high a temperature.
items.fix: The covered phase is what keeps the ribs moist. Seal the foil tightly. If the ribs are already dry, serve with the pan juices spooned over, or cider vinegar on the side.

items.cause: Rub scorched during the uncovered phase.
items.fix: The uncovered phase at 180°C should be no more than 30 minutes. Check after 20 minutes: if the surface looks very dark, pull them out.

items.symptom: The membrane didn't come off cleanly
items.cause: Grip failed, or the membrane tore.
items.fix: Even a few pieces of membrane left on are fine: they just become slightly chewy. Use kitchen paper rather than a cloth, and pull slowly.

content.text: Memphis is one of the four great American barbecue traditions, alongside Kansas City, Carolina, and Texas. Its defining contribution is the dry rib: no sauce, just rub. The spice blend is more complex than the Texas salt-and-pepper style, using paprika, chilli powder, celery salt, and mustard powder. Dry ribs and wet (sauced) ribs are both on the menu in Memphis.
